clinicalPearls: A rare but almost uniformly fatal complication caused by viable donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking recipient tissues.

Occurs when the recipient cannot reject donor lymphocytes, either through immunosuppression or when the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype the recipient carries, as in directed donations from relatives.
Typically presents one to six weeks after transfusion with fever, a maculopapular rash, diarrhoea, deranged liver function and progressive pancytopenia.
The defining and lethal feature is marrow aplasia, distinguishing it from graft-versus-host disease after stem-cell transplantation where the graft marrow is spared.
Gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular components to inactivate donor lymphocytes is the mainstay of prevention; leucoreduction alone is insufficient.
At-risk groups include recipients of directed donations from first-degree relatives, HLA-matched platelets, intrauterine or neonatal exchange transfusions, and the severely immunocompromised.
Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy and by demonstrating donor-derived lymphocytes or chimerism in the recipient.
Established disease responds poorly to immunosuppression, underscoring that prevention is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease results from immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes that are transfused within a cellular blood component and are not eliminated by the recipient's immune system. These viable donor lymphocytes recognise recipient HLA antigens as foreign, proliferate and mount a cytotoxic attack against host tissues bearing those antigens, principally skin, gut, liver and, critically, the bone marrow. Engraftment is favoured either by profound recipient immunosuppression or by a one-way HLA match, in which the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype shared with the recipient so that the recipient does not perceive the donor cells as foreign while the donor cells still attack the recipient. The consequent immune destruction of the marrow produces intractable aplasia and overwhelming infection.
additionalDifferentials: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms or other drug eruption
Viral infection such as cytomegalovirus with marrow suppression
Graft-versus-host disease after haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing basal vacuolar change, dyskeratosis and lymphocytic infiltrate
Bone marrow examination demonstrating hypoplasia or aplasia
HLA typing and chimerism studies to detect donor lymphocytes in recipient blood or tissue
Full blood count tracking progressive pancytopenia
Liver function tests documenting cholestatic derangement
Review of transfusion history for non-irradiated cellular components in an at-risk recipient
redFlags: Progressive pancytopenia developing one to six weeks after transfusion
Fever with rash, diarrhoea and deranged liver function in an at-risk recipient
Transfusion of non-irradiated components to a severely immunocompromised patient
Receipt of a directed donation from a blood relative
Marrow aplasia without an alternative explanation
reference.prognosis: The condition is almost always fatal, usually within weeks, from marrow failure with overwhelming infection and bleeding, because established disease responds poorly to treatment. This dismal outlook makes irradiation of at-risk cellular components the essential intervention.
pitfalls: Assuming leucoreduction alone prevents the disease when irradiation is required.
Failing to identify at-risk recipients who require irradiated components.
Overlooking the danger of directed donations from first-degree relatives.
Attributing the rash, diarrhoea and cytopenia to drugs or infection and delaying diagnosis.
Expecting immunosuppressive treatment to reverse established disease.
references: British Society for Haematology guidelines on the use of irradiated blood components
Mollison's Blood Transfusion in Clinical Medicine
management: Prevention is the essential intervention: gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular blood components for at-risk recipients, since leucoreduction alone is insufficient

Identify and flag at-risk groups including the severely immunocompromised, recipients of directed donations from relatives, HLA-matched platelets, and intrauterine or neonatal exchange transfusions, so they always receive irradiated components
Attempt aggressive immunosuppression with corticosteroids, ciclosporin and antithymocyte globulin for established disease, recognising response is generally poor
Intensive supportive care for the resulting marrow aplasia, including transfusion support, haematopoietic growth factors and management of skin, gut and hepatic involvement
Aggressive prophylaxis and treatment of infection, as overwhelming infection with bleeding drives the near-uniform mortality
Consider haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in rare, appropriately selected cases, involving transfusion medicine and haematology throughout
